steps.explanationAfterStep: The negative charge sits mostly on oxygen. The C–H next to a ketone has a pKa of about 20, low enough for hydroxide to remove a little of it at a time.
The slow step: the conjugate base loses the leaving group. The new C=C bond is conjugated with C=O, which pays for losing a poor leaving group. Hydroxide is regenerated: it is a catalyst.

title: E1cB: diacetone alcohol to mesityl oxide
subtitle: An enolate pushes out hydroxide
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapters 17 and 26

enolate.caption: the enolate + water
hintTiers: Electrons from the enolate oxygen can flow along the C=C bond towards the carbon carrying the OH.
The oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O, the C=C π bond moves one bond along, and the C–OH bond breaks onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Enolate oxygen lone pair → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=C π bond → a π bond to the carbon carrying OH; the C–OH bond → a lone pair on that oxygen.
enolate.learnerPrompt: The enolate pushes out the leaving group.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton back just reverses the first step. Let the enolate push hydroxide out instead.
That would make a strained four-membered ring. The enolate's electrons flow along the C=C bond to push hydroxide out.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide does leave here, but only because the enolate pushes it. Add the arrows from the enolate oxygen and the C=C bond.

reactants.caption: diacetone alcohol (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one) + sodium hydroxide
hintTiers: A C–H next to a C=O group is acidic: the negative charge of its conjugate base can sit on oxygen.
Hydroxide takes the drawn hydrogen on the CH₂ between the two functional groups. The C–H electrons form a C=C bond and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → the drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide is a base. Which proton is acidic? Form the enolate.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so a concerted E2 is not possible. The C–H next to the ketone is acidic: form the enolate first.
Hydroxide will not leave on its own from a neutral molecule, and there is no acid to protonate it. Make the enolate first: its electrons will push hydroxide out.
Hydroxide can add to the ketone, but that only gives an unstable hydrate that falls apart again. Here hydroxide acts as a base.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the base takes the proton and a C=C forms. The carbonyl carbon now has five bonds: move the C=O π electrons onto oxygen.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide removes a proton from the carbon next to the ketone: that C–H is acidic because the enolate it gives is stabilised by the C=O group. The enolate (the conjugate base, the cB of E1cB) then pushes out hydroxide from the next carbon, forming the conjugated enone, mesityl oxide. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, but the conjugated C=C–C=O product makes this step favourable. This is the second half of an aldol condensation.
